items.prompt: What does a level primarily measure in this unit?
choices: The size of problems you treat as yours without being told
How many years you have spent in the role or at the company overall
The hardest defined problem you can solve on your own
items.explanation: A level scores scope: how much ambiguity you resolve unasked, not tenure and not raw difficulty solved.

items.prompt: Which question does skill answer?
choices: What is the largest ambiguity this person resolved unasked?
How far do other teams change habits because of them?
Given a well-defined problem, can this person solve it?
items.explanation: Skill is about solving a problem once it is defined.

items.prompt: Which question does scope answer?
choices: Given a well-defined hard problem, can this person solve it correctly once?
What is the largest ambiguity this person resolved without being asked?
How quickly does this person fix a bug that was assigned to them?
items.explanation: Scope is about deciding what needs solving, which is a different axis from solving it.

items.prompt: Is skill irrelevant to leveling?
choices: No, it makes wider scope possible but does not prove it
Yes, only scope matters and skill is never examined at any stage
Yes, but only after the first promotion decision
items.explanation: Skill is one input to scope. It is correlated with scope, just not identical to it.

items.prompt: Sam climbs the hardest routes but only ones already set. Riley started a beginner session nobody asked for. Whose evidence is about scope?
choices: Sam's, because the hardest routes are the biggest problems
Neither, because both are only doing their own climbing
Riley's, because the session was not assigned
items.explanation: Starting something nobody assigned is scope evidence. Clearing hard set routes is skill evidence.

items.prompt: Which of these is evidence of scope rather than skill?
choices: Fixing an assigned bug on the first attempt
Picking up a problem nobody owned
Knowing a programming language in great depth
items.explanation: Scope shows up as ambiguity resolved unasked. The other two are about skill on a defined task.

items.prompt: How are skill and scope related?
choices: Correlated but not the same measurement
They are the same measurement under two names
They are completely unrelated to each other
items.explanation: Skill helps make wider scope possible, but each answers a different question.

items.prompt: Two people started in the same week. Are they automatically at the same level?
choices: Yes, starting together puts them at the same level
Yes, unless one of them is more skilled
No, tenure alone does not set a level
items.explanation: A level reflects the scope someone operates at, not when they started.

items.prompt: Priya is the fastest on her team at fixing assigned bugs. Marcus is slower, but noticed nobody owned the release-notes tooling and fixed it. Which reading fits this unit's framework best?
choices: Priya's speed shows she handles wider scope than Marcus does, since fast fixes count most
Marcus's story is stronger scope evidence; Priya's is strong skill evidence
Both stories are scope evidence, so they count about equally toward a level conversation
Neither story counts at all, since levels in this framework follow time served alone
items.explanation: Taking on an unowned problem is scope. Fast execution of assigned bugs is skill. Both are real, but they answer different questions.
items.reference:
Skill and scope answer different questions
skill: can you solve it once it is defined?
scope: did you decide what needed solving?
a level looks mainly at the second
Why: a level scores the size of problems you treated as yours, and skill only makes that possible.
items.learnMore:
Skill is an input, scope is the measure

Skill makes wider scope possible, but a highly skilled person who only receives defined tasks has shown skill, not scope. Evidence of scope is ambiguity resolved without being asked.

Common mistake

Reading a strong skill record as proof of wide scope. They are correlated, not identical.
items.reflection: Think of someone you know who is excellent at their craft. What is the largest thing they decided needed doing without anyone asking?

items.prompt: An engineer argues: "My code-quality review scores are the best on the team, so I deserve the next level." What is the gap in that argument?
choices: It is sound, since the best code on a team always signals the widest scope of work
Review scores are too subjective to count, so there is no evidence at all
It shows skill on defined work, while scope asks about problems nobody defined
It needs a longer tenure first, since review scores only count after several more years
items.explanation: Review scores support the skill term. A level conversation asks whether that skill was applied to ambiguity nobody assigned.

choices: Scope is just skill averaged over the last few years of a person's work history
Skill and scope are independent, so skill has no bearing on wider scope at all
Scope is only a polite word for how senior a title sounds
A highly skilled person kept on assigned tasks has not yet shown wide scope

items.prompt: Someone early in their skill development quietly notices that nobody tracks the team's recurring outages and starts a simple log. What does this unit's framework say?
choices: They show real scope, even if their skill is still developing
They show nothing yet, because scope requires expert skill first
They show only skill, since writing a log is a routine task
They show scope only if their title was already raised
items.explanation: Scope is about resolving ambiguity nobody assigned. Someone earlier in skill can already do that, which is why skill and scope are separate axes.

items.prompt: Which dimension asks what breaks, and how widely, if your decision is wrong?
choices: Time horizon
Blast radius
Ambiguity tolerance
items.explanation: Blast radius is the reach of damage from a wrong call.

items.prompt: Which dimension asks how undefined the problem is when it reaches you?
choices: Ambiguity tolerance
Influence radius
Blast radius of a call
items.explanation: Ambiguity tolerance measures how much unclear problem you can make sense of.

items.prompt: A fix that will not matter for a year is mostly a statement about which dimension?
choices: Blast radius
Influence radius
Time horizon
items.explanation: Time horizon is about when the problem or payoff shows up.

items.prompt: Which dimension asks who changes behavior because of your work?
choices: Ambiguity tolerance
Influence radius
Time horizon
items.explanation: Influence radius covers only you, your team, or people outside it.

items.prompt: Riley's beginner guide could mislead every newcomer who reads it if it were wrong. Which dimension is that?
choices: Blast radius
Time horizon
Influence radius
items.explanation: The question is how far damage spreads if the guide is wrong, which is blast radius.

items.prompt: Two other teams adopt a convention you proposed, unprompted. Which dimension grew?
choices: Blast radius
Ambiguity tolerance
Influence radius
items.explanation: Other people changing behavior because of your work is influence radius.

items.prompt: Monitoring that will only matter a year from now is evidence for which dimension?
choices: Blast radius
Time horizon
Influence radius
items.explanation: It looks past this week's problem, so it is a wide time horizon.

items.prompt: How many scope dimensions does this unit name?
choices: Four
Three
Six
items.explanation: Ambiguity tolerance, blast radius, time horizon and influence radius.

items.prompt: A manager hands someone the sentence "users are churning and we do not know why". Which dimension does that mainly stretch?
choices: Time horizon of the payoff
Blast radius if it fails
Ambiguity tolerance
Influence radius over teams
items.explanation: Nothing about the problem is defined yet, so the person must define it first. That is ambiguity tolerance.
items.reference:
Four questions, one per dimension
ambiguity: how undefined is it on arrival?
blast radius: how far does a wrong call spread?
time horizon: when does it stop mattering?
influence: who changes habits because of you?
Why: each dimension is a separate question, so a profile can be wide on some and narrow on others.
items.learnMore:
Four separate dimensions

Ambiguity is about the problem, blast radius about the damage of a wrong call, time horizon about how long the effect lasts, and influence radius about who changes behavior. They tend to widen together but are different.

Common mistake

Confusing blast radius with influence radius. One is damage if you are wrong; the other is who adopts your work.
items.reflection: Pick something you recently did. Which of the four questions would you answer widest, and which narrowest?

items.prompt: An engineer's design choice on a shared service would break every consuming team if wrong, but nobody outside her team has ever changed habits because of her. What profile is that?
choices: Narrow blast radius with a wide influence radius
Wide on both, since both involve other teams
Narrow on both, since her own team is unchanged
Wide blast radius with a narrow influence radius
items.explanation: Blast radius is damage if wrong; influence radius is who adopts your work. Here the first is wide and the second is not.

items.prompt: A migration has a complete spec and an unambiguous owner, but will not pay off for 18 months. Which combination fits?
choices: Narrow ambiguity but a wide time horizon
Wide ambiguity but a narrow time horizon
Narrow on both, since the spec is complete
Wide on both, since the payoff is far away
items.explanation: A clear spec means little ambiguity to resolve. The long payoff is what makes the horizon wide.

A narrow blast radius with a high ambiguity
A narrow blast radius with a clear definition
A wide influence radius with a clear definition
items.explanation: Only their own file is at risk, so blast radius is narrow, while not knowing where to start is a mark of ambiguity.

items.prompt: At which stage has someone else already resolved the ambiguity before it reaches you?
choices: Stage C, a problem with no owner
Stage D, direction across teams
Stage A, a well-defined task
items.explanation: At stage A the spec and the owner already exist.

items.prompt: At which stage do you fill gaps in an unclear spec?
choices: Stage A, a well-defined task with an owner
Stage B, a project with unclear edges
Stage D, direction across teams
items.explanation: Stage B means the edges are fuzzy and you close them.

items.prompt: At which stage do you decide that a problem needs solving at all?
choices: Stage C, a problem with no owner yet
Stage A, a well-defined task
Stage B, a project with unclear edges
items.explanation: Nobody has been assigned the problem, so recognizing it is your work.

items.prompt: At which stage do you shape what problems get worked on across teams?
choices: Stage B, a project with unclear edges
Stage A, a well-defined task
Stage D, direction across teams
items.explanation: Stage D is about setting direction, not only executing it.

items.prompt: Does someone at stage D stop doing well-defined tasks?
choices: Yes, those are left to earlier stages
No, they still do them sometimes
Yes, but only on weekdays
items.explanation: The stages are about what is expected by default, not about skills being dropped.

items.prompt: Is staying at stage A a moral failing?
choices: No, a clear task can be the right scope
Yes, every person must climb to stage D
Yes, unless the task is easy
items.explanation: The scale describes typical scope, not worth.

items.prompt: What is the order of the stages, from narrowest to widest?
choices: Project, task, cross-team direction, unowned problem
Unowned problem, task, project, cross-team direction
Task, project, unowned problem, cross-team direction
items.explanation: Each stage widens the boundary of what you treat as yours.

items.prompt: In the gym story, which action matches stage C?
choices: Climbing a route that is already set and graded
Noticing nobody explains grades and starting to
Following a coach's plan for a fixed session
items.explanation: Nobody owned the gap, and Riley decided it needed solving.

items.prompt: Dana is named owner of "make onboarding smoother" with no spec. Everyone agrees it matters, and it is hers. Which stage best fits?
choices: Stage A, since a named owner makes it a defined task
Stage C, since the ambiguity makes the problem unowned
Stage D, since onboarding touches several teams
Stage B, since she owns it and must fill the gaps
items.explanation: An owner exists, so it is not unowned, but the edges are unclear. That is the project stage.
items.reference:
Stages A to D
A: well-defined task, someone else defined it
B: project with unclear edges, you fill gaps
C: problem with no owner, you decide it matters
D: direction across teams, you shape the agenda
Why: each stage changes what is expected by default, not which skills you lose.
items.learnMore:
Stages describe defaults, not worth

At every stage you still do the earlier kinds of work. What changes is who has already resolved the ambiguity before the problem reaches you, and how much of that is expected of you.

Common mistake

Treating stage A as a failure. A clear task can be exactly the right scope for a real need.
items.reflection: Where in your current work is someone else still resolving the ambiguity before it reaches you? What would change if you resolved it yourself?

items.prompt: What changes most between an engineer at stage A and one at stage D?
choices: What is expected by default, since resolving unassigned ambiguity becomes the job
Their ability to write code, which stops being needed once they reach stage D work
Their willingness to work hard, which engineers at stage A are said to lack entirely
The number of meetings they attend, which is the only real difference between stages
items.explanation: Stage D engineers still write code and do defined work. The default expectation shifts toward resolving ambiguity nobody assigned.

It is correct, since scope is the only quality that any leveling process rewards
It is wrong, since the stages never describe real work
items.explanation: The scale is descriptive. Clean delivery of defined tasks is real value, and the stage becomes relevant only for the level being compared.

Stage D, because she is shaping what several teams work on
Stage C, because the problem concerns only her own team's tooling
items.explanation: The work spans teams and sets a shared direction, which is the cross-team stage.

items.prompt: Is it typical to be wide on all four dimensions the day you are promoted?
choices: No, scope usually widens one dimension at a time
Yes, all four dimensions move together on that day
Yes, but only if the promotion is a large one
items.explanation: Expansion is typically uneven, not simultaneous.

items.prompt: Is being wide on blast radius but narrow on influence unusual?
choices: Yes, it never happens in real careers
Yes, unless the two are about the same task
No, uneven profiles are common
items.explanation: Uneven expansion is the normal pattern.

items.prompt: In the demo, ambiguity, blast radius and time horizon start at 3 and influence at 2. How does influence compare with the average of 2.75?
choices: It sits 0.75 above it
It sits 0.75 below it
It equals the average exactly
items.explanation: 2 minus 2.75 is minus 0.75.

items.prompt: In the demo, influence is dragged to 10 while the others stay at 3. How does influence compare with the new average?
choices: It sits 5.25 above it
It sits 7 above it
It sits 4.75 above it
items.explanation: The average becomes 4.75, and 10 minus 4.75 is 5.25.

items.prompt: Is the demo a promotion formula?
choices: Yes, it is the exact formula used
Yes, but only for influence radius
No, it is a teaching model
items.explanation: It exists to show how uneven a profile can be, not to decide promotions.

items.prompt: Why is one average a poor summary of a scope profile?
choices: It always gives the same number for every person's profile
It hides which dimensions are wide and which are narrow
It is too hard to compute for four values
items.explanation: Different profiles can produce the same average, so the shape is lost.

items.prompt: Is an uneven profile a sign you answered the exercise wrongly?
choices: No, the unevenness is itself informative
Yes, a correct profile has four equal values
Yes, unless it is slightly uneven
items.explanation: The unevenness tells you where evidence is still missing.

items.prompt: Leveling is better described as which of these?
choices: One magic average of four separate scores
A ranking of raw technical skill
A profile of evidence across dimensions
items.explanation: The point of the unit is to read evidence across dimensions, not to produce a single number.

items.prompt: Person X is 9 on ambiguity, 2 on blast radius, 2 on time horizon and 3 on influence. Person Y is 4 on all four. Both average 4. What does this unit's model say?
choices: The same average hides very different shapes, so read evidence per dimension
They sit at the same level, since the two averages match exactly at 4
Person X is clearly wider, since one of the four scores is far higher
Person Y is clearly wider, since none of the four scores is low at all
items.explanation: An average erases the shape. The unit's point is that leveling reads a profile of evidence, not one number.
items.reference:
An average hides the shape
profile: 3, 3, 3, 2 gives average 2.75
raise influence to 10: average only 4.75
influence sits 5.25 above its own average
Why: one axis moving a lot barely moves the average, so evidence must be read per dimension.
items.learnMore:
A profile of evidence

Scope usually widens one dimension at a time, so being wide on one and narrow on another is normal. The teaching model in the demo is not a promotion formula; it shows why one number misleads.

Common mistake

Treating the average as the answer. Two very different profiles can share the same average.
items.reflection: Sketch your own four dimensions from narrow to wide. Which one is furthest from the others, and what evidence would move it?

items.prompt: Ambiguity, blast radius and time horizon stay at 3 while influence rises from 2 to 6. By how much does the average move, and what does that show?

It moves by 1.0, a quarter of influence's rise, so the average hides it
It moves by 0.75, which shows influence barely changed in this case at all
It does not move at all, since the other three dimensions stay fixed
items.explanation: Average goes from 2.75 to 3.75, a rise of 1.0. A big move on one axis is mostly invisible in the average.

items.prompt: This unit calls a title which kind of indicator?
choices: A lagging indicator
A leading indicator
A random indicator
items.explanation: The label trails the scope someone already operates at.

items.prompt: How are titles typically assigned?
choices: Instantly when scope widens, with no review process involved
By the engineer choosing their own
Through a review or promotion process on a cadence
items.explanation: Titles come from a scheduled process, so they can trail real scope.

items.prompt: How does real scope expansion usually happen?
choices: In one step at each review
Continuously and unevenly
Only at a promotion committee
items.explanation: It grows as people take on more, long before any review.

items.prompt: Someone works wider than their title says. What has happened?
choices: The title has not caught up yet
The framework has been disproven
The person has lost scope
items.explanation: This is the lagging indicator doing what the unit predicts.

items.prompt: When can a title be ahead of real scope?
choices: Only after a failed project or a missed deadline
Never, titles always match
After a lateral hire or a retention raise
items.explanation: Titles can be set by hiring or retention reasons, not by demonstrated scope.

items.prompt: Does a mismatch between title and scope mean the framework is wrong?
choices: Yes, the framework always requires title and scope to match
No, a lagging indicator is expected to disagree sometimes
Yes, unless the mismatch is small
items.explanation: The framework predicts these gaps.

items.prompt: Which analogy does the unit use for a title?
choices: A grade posted after an exam period
A key that opens the next door
A map drawn before the trip
items.explanation: The work happens first and the official label arrives later.

items.prompt: Do two companies always use a title to mean the same standard?
choices: Yes, titles are standardized across every company worldwide
Yes, within the same industry
No, the same label can mean a slightly different standard
items.explanation: Titles vary across companies, one more reason a title is not the definition of scope.

items.prompt: Dana has worked at much wider scope for months but was not promoted at the last review cycle. What is the best explanation consistent with this unit?
choices: Her scope was not real until a title confirmed it for her
Title trails scope because reviews run on a cadence
The framework is wrong, since a title and scope must always match
Her skill dropped, so her scope shrank to match the old title
items.explanation: Scope grows continuously while titles update on a schedule. A gap is expected, not proof she lacks the scope.
items.reference:
Work first, label later
scope widens continuously, unevenly
review cycle runs quarterly or yearly
title updates after, sometimes noisily

items.prompt: Is Response 1, fixing exactly the reported leak, wrong?
choices: Yes, it ignores the wider pattern that the engineer saw
No, it is complete, correct work for a defined task
Yes, it breaks the team's rules
items.explanation: Nothing is wrong with Response 1. It is scoped to a defined task.

items.prompt: What justified Response 2's lint rule?
choices: The same pattern appeared in three other files
A hunch that other bugs might exist
A request from the platform team
items.explanation: The engineer acted on evidence found while investigating.

items.prompt: What is scope creep, as this unit uses it?
choices: Any work beyond the literal ticket, even when evidence supports it
Reporting a bug nobody asked about
Speculative extra work with no evidence the problem is real
items.explanation: Creep is widening by guess. Widening on evidence is expansion.

items.prompt: What makes real expansion different from creep?
choices: It always involves more people than the original ticket did
Each addition is directly evidenced by what was found
It always takes more calendar time
items.explanation: Evidence is the test, not size or duration.

items.prompt: Declining to flag a pattern you have clearly seen, to stay in your lane, is described as what?
choices: Withholding useful information, a common way to plateau
A sign of humility that the whole team values and rewards
The safest way to earn a wider scope
items.explanation: The unit calls out that staying silent about a seen pattern is not modesty.

items.prompt: Across the four responses, what mostly stays the same?
choices: The number of people involved across the response
The time horizon of the work
The technical fact and the skill to fix the leak
items.explanation: The code does not get harder. The boundary of 'my problem' widens.

items.prompt: While fixing an unrelated login bug, an engineer decides to rewrite the whole authentication system just in case. What is this?
choices: Scope expansion, since it is a wider fix
Scope creep, since no evidence supports the rewrite
A defined task, since login was assigned
items.explanation: A rewrite with no evidence of a wider problem is creep.

items.prompt: What unowned problem did Response 3 identify?
choices: No trend alerting, so slow leaks were hidden
A missing lint rule in the build
A shortage of staff on the platform team
items.explanation: Auto-restart had masked the leak's growth curve for months.

items.prompt: While fixing a small login bug, an engineer rewrites the entire authentication layer because it "might hide more bugs". How does this unit classify it?
choices: Scope expansion, since the work reaches a bigger system
A defined task, since login was the assigned area
Scope creep, since nothing found points to a wider problem
Platform direction, since authentication affects many users
items.explanation: Expansion needs evidence from what you found. A guess that more bugs might exist is not evidence.
items.reference:
Evidence separates expansion from creep
expansion: the pattern appeared in three files
creep: rewrite everything, just in case
plateau: saw the pattern, said nothing
Why: wider work is justified when what you found points to a wider problem.
items.learnMore:
Evidence is the test

Each addition in the leak story followed from something the engineer actually found. Without that evidence, the same widening becomes speculative scope creep, while refusing to widen at all can be a quiet plateau.

Common mistake

Equating widening with progress. Widening without evidence is creep.
items.reflection: Recall a time you added extra work to a task. What evidence in front of you justified it, or was it a guess?

items.prompt: Suppose the leak had already caused a customer-facing outage. What does the evidence rule imply about extra work?
choices: Urgency removes the need for evidence on any extra work that gets proposed
Nothing changes, so only the literal leak may be touched until it recurs
The outage makes org-wide changes immediately justified for the engineer
The outage supports related work, but unrelated rewrites still need evidence
items.explanation: An outage is itself evidence of impact, which supports closely related fixes. It does not turn guesses about unrelated systems into evidence.

items.prompt: What does cross-team influence depend on, per this unit?
choices: A title that is higher than the titles held by everyone in the audience
How many times the idea is repeated in a row
Credibility built through consistent smaller-scope delivery
items.explanation: Influence across teams rests on a record of delivering.

items.prompt: A platform proposal comes from someone with no delivery record. What might the platform team reasonably doubt?
choices: Whether the proposed platform change exists in other firms
The proposer's follow-through, not just the idea
Whether any engineer may speak
items.explanation: Without a record, nobody can judge whether the proposer will carry it through.

items.prompt: Is one standout Response 3 incident proof of consistently wide scope?
choices: No, one incident is a single data point
Yes, one incident settles the level
Yes, if it was recent
items.explanation: Leveling looks at patterns across many situations.

items.prompt: Is one Response 1 fix a permanent cap on someone's level?
choices: Yes, it fixes their level for good
Yes, within the same quarter
No, one narrow fix does not cap anyone
items.explanation: A single data point in either direction misleads.

items.prompt: What do leveling conversations look at?
choices: The single most recent incident
A pattern across many situations
The title that was given first
items.explanation: A pattern is more reliable than one example.

items.prompt: Which delivery should come before attempting an org-wide default?
choices: Reliable Response 2 and 3 level work
Only Response 1 level fixes
A bigger title than the platform team's
items.explanation: The unit sequences smaller-scope delivery before a cross-team proposal.

items.prompt: A single data point can mislead in which direction?
choices: Only upward, overstating scope and never understating it
Only too low
In both directions, too high and too low
items.explanation: One incident can overstate or understate someone's scope.

items.prompt: Is attempting Response 4 early, before any smaller delivery, listed as a failure mode?
choices: No, it is the recommended first step
Yes, as attempting it without earned trust
No, only the idea matters
items.explanation: Cross-team influence is built on credibility from smaller work.

items.prompt: Two engineers submit near-identical platform proposals. One has 18 months of reliable smaller-scope delivery and the other has none. Which is more likely to be adopted, and why?
choices: The one without a record, because fresh ideas are valued more highly
Both equally, because the two proposals read the same on the page
Neither, because platform changes like this never get adopted anywhere
The one with the record, because their follow-through is credible
items.explanation: Cross-team influence rests on credibility. The record lowers the doubt about carrying the proposal through.
items.reference:
Credibility and patterns, not single moments
wide proposal + reliable smaller deliveries: trusted
wide proposal + no record: doubted
one incident: a data point, not a level
Why: cross-team influence rests on follow-through, and a level reads a pattern.
items.learnMore:
Earned, not claimed

A platform-wide proposal from someone with no record of delivering smaller work invites doubt about follow-through, not necessarily about the idea. And any one incident, good or bad, is a single data point.

Common mistake

Judging a level from one standout success or one narrow fix.
